newsitem.title: CANADA: Sudan awards oil concession to Canada's IPC.
newsitem.headline: Sudan awards oil concession to Canada's IPC.

text.p: Canada's International Petroleum Corp. said on Thursday it was awarded a high-profile oil concession in Sudan, but the company will have to develop the property without the aid of a big U.S. partner.

Los Angeles-based Occidental Petroleum Corp. had been widely expected to be part of the deal, but the prospect of its involvement has faded over the past 10 days amid growing controversy over U.S. anti-terrorist legislation.

IPC of Vancouver, British Columbia, said the Block 5A concession, which adjoins acreage being developed by an international consortium including Calgary-based Arakis Energy Corp. covered 29,412 square km (11,356 sqare miles) in an area previously operated by Chevron Corp.
The Arakis concession was estimated by Chevron to harbour as much as 3.5 billion barrels of oil, and Arakis has made several discoveries over the past two years.
IPC director Lukas Lundin said he believed the huge 5A block could hold a similar prize.
"It's an extension of the same thing. It's still exploration, but I'd be extremely surprised if we didn't find the same structures," Lundin said in an interview.

Lundin said partners taking part in the deal were not yet finalised. But informed sources said the agreement would include IPC with 65 percent, Malaysia state oil company Petronas with 30 percent and the Sudan government with 5 percent. Petronas is also a partner in the $1 billion Arakis deal.

Occidental -- which had earlier been reported negotiating for a stake in the Arakis transaction before being ejected from the talks by the Sudanese government -- was later rumoured to be in serious discussions with IPC for the block.
IPC appeared so sure it would be working with a major U.S. company on the project that it mentioned in its recently released annual report that a 50-50 agreement with one was in place.

One source close to the deal said Occidental was indeed involved with IPC until Jan. 28, five days after the Washington Post ran a front-page story about Sudan being exempted from broad sanctions in the U.S. Anti-terrorism Act while five other blacklisted nations were not.
The story suggested the exemption cleared the way for Occidental to negotiate its way into the Arakis deal, an allegation denied by U.S. government officials.
Arakis announced late last year that its partners would be China National Petroleum Corp., Petronas and the Sudan government.

IPC said a 1,500 km (932-mile) pipeline being planned by the Arakis group would provide it with an export route for any production on the block. The firm is also considering the possibility of buying an equity stake in the proposed line, slated to be completed by 1999.

"IPC plans to embark immediately upon an aggressive programme of exploration activity in the block including the acquisition of 1,350 km (839 miles) of new seismic data and the likelihood of drilling the first exploration well by the end of 1997," the company said.
